lessons.title: Core Microsoft 365 objects and how they relate
lessons.summary: Map users, groups, licenses, mailboxes, SharePoint sites, Teams, OneDrive, and admin centers to common administration tasks.
learningObjectives: Map users, groups, licenses, mailboxes, sites, Teams, and OneDrive to admin tasks
Describe how Teams and SharePoint sites support collaboration workspaces
Identify admin centers used to manage Microsoft 365 core objects
Choose the right Microsoft 365 object for a collaboration scenario
lessons.explanation: Microsoft 365 core objects start with users, groups, licenses, mailboxes, sites, Teams, and OneDrive. A **user** is the identity that signs in and receives licenses. A **Microsoft 365 group** can connect collaboration resources such as mailbox, calendar, SharePoint files, Planner, and Teams. A **security group** is usually for access assignment and policy targeting. A **distribution list** routes email. Exchange admins manage mailboxes and distribution groups; SharePoint admins manage sites, libraries, folders, and permissions; Teams admins manage teams, channels, and policies. Licenses assigned to users or groups determine which Microsoft 365 features are available. Contoso Field Services uses this map before changing anything: person, group, collaboration space, mail object, file location, Teams policy, and license.

terminology.definition: An identity that signs in and can receive licenses, roles, and group memberships.
A collaboration membership object that can connect several Microsoft 365 services.
A group commonly used for permissions, app access, and policy targeting.
A mail-enabled list used to send messages to many recipients.
A workspace for pages, libraries, folders, and permissions.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso Field Services is opening a West region repair crew. Priya must decide whether each request belongs to a user account, Microsoft 365 group, security group, distribution list, shared mailbox, SharePoint site, Team, channel, or OneDrive location before she assigns licenses.
lessons.technicalExample: Object map for the West crew: `Priya` is a user; `Repair Crew West` is a Microsoft 365 group; `Repair Crew West Team` contains channels; `Repair Manuals` is a SharePoint library; `dispatch@contoso.example` is a shared mailbox; `West-App-Access` is a security group.

misconception.myth: A distribution list is a lightweight replacement for a Team, SharePoint site, or Microsoft 365 group.
misconception.reality: A distribution list routes email. Team collaboration needs membership, files, conversations, permissions, and often a Microsoft 365 group-backed workspace.

lessons.examTakeaway: If the scenario says mailbox or distribution group, think Exchange. If it says sites, libraries, folders, or permissions, think SharePoint. If it says teams, channels, or policies, think Teams. If it says access targeting, compare security groups and Microsoft 365 groups.
lessons.recap: Map users, groups, licenses, mailboxes, SharePoint sites, Teams, OneDrive, and admin centers to common administration tasks.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Picture a community center: users are member cards, Microsoft 365 groups are clubs, distribution lists are announcement megaphones, SharePoint is the file cabinet room, Teams is the meeting room, and OneDrive is each person's backpack.
lessons.anotherExample: Fabrikam uses a distribution list for outage announcements, a shared mailbox for supplier invoices, a security group for a scheduling app, and a Microsoft 365 group with Teams for the project crew.

lessons.title: Microsoft 365 security principles
lessons.summary: Explain Zero Trust, least privilege, authentication, authorization, threat protection, intelligence, and Defender XDR.
learningObjectives: Explain Zero Trust principles of verify explicitly and assume breach
Identify least-privilege actions that reduce Microsoft 365 risk
Distinguish authentication, authorization, and threat protection concepts
Recognize how Defender XDR and threat intelligence support security
lessons.explanation: Microsoft 365 security principles are easier when you separate identity proof from permission. **Authentication** proves who a user or workload is; **authorization** decides what that identity can do. **Zero Trust** says verify explicitly, use least privilege, and assume breach. That means access decisions consider signals such as user, device, location, application, and risk instead of trusting a network forever. Threat protection and intelligence help teams detect and investigate suspicious activity. Microsoft Defender XDR coordinates protection signals across Microsoft security workloads, while admins still own configuration, role design, policies, and response. Contoso uses least privilege so a reports reader is not made a permanent Global Administrator.

terminology.definition: Verify explicitly, use least privilege, and assume breach.
The decision about what an identity may access.
Grant only the access needed for the task.
Context that helps identify and respond to threats.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso technicians sign in from customer sites, hotels, and home networks. Alex must design access decisions that verify identity, limit privileges, and still let field work continue.
lessons.technicalExample: Access review row: `Signal=risky sign-in for technician`; `Authentication=require MFA`; `Authorization=work-order app only`; `Threat review=Defender XDR incident and sign-in logs`; `Follow-up=remove unused privileged roles`.

misconception.myth: Zero Trust means every user is blocked unless they are in the office.
misconception.reality: Zero Trust means every request is evaluated with explicit signals and least privilege. Trusted work can continue when the right controls are satisfied.

lessons.examTakeaway: Separate the verbs: authenticate proves identity, authorize grants an action, least privilege narrows access, assume breach drives monitoring, and threat protection helps detect and respond.
lessons.recap: Explain Zero Trust, least privilege, authentication, authorization, threat protection, intelligence, and Defender XDR.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Think of a concert venue. Authentication checks the ticket and face, authorization decides whether the person can enter backstage, least privilege gives only the right wristband, and security staff keep watching after entry.
lessons.anotherExample: Woodgrove Bank lets support staff reset passwords with a specific role, but requires stronger authentication and review before anyone activates a privileged security role.

lessons.title: Core Microsoft 365 security features
lessons.summary: Identify MFA, Conditional Access, Defender for Office 365, Secure Score, admin roles, PIM, audit logs, app registrations, and enterprise applications.
learningObjectives: Identify MFA, Conditional Access, and admin roles for stronger access control
Describe how Defender for Office 365 helps protect against email threats
Explain how Secure Score, PIM, and audit logs support administration
Distinguish app registrations from enterprise applications in Microsoft Entra
lessons.explanation: Core Microsoft 365 security features protect sign-ins, email, collaboration, posture, and privileged tasks. Microsoft Entra ID provides identity capabilities. MFA adds more proof than a password alone. Conditional Access evaluates signals and can allow, block, or require controls such as MFA. SSO improves user experience while still respecting policies. For sign-in troubleshooting, review MFA results, Conditional Access results, risky sign-ins, and audit/sign-in logs. Microsoft Defender for Office 365 protects email and collaboration from phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Secure Score and Identity Secure Score help prioritize improvements. Admin roles, PIM, app registrations, and enterprise applications support controlled administration and app access.

terminology.definition: Authentication using more than one factor.
A policy engine that evaluates signals and applies controls.
Protection for email and collaboration threats.
A posture measurement and recommendation experience.

lessons.businessScenario: Contoso receives a phishing report, a blocked admin sign-in, and a request for a posture improvement plan on the same morning. Priya must pick the feature that answers each symptom.
lessons.technicalExample: Troubleshooting note: `Symptom=admin blocked`; `Evidence=sign-in log and Conditional Access result`; `Control=MFA required`; `Posture follow-up=review Identity Secure Score`; `Threat follow-up=Defender for Office 365 investigation if mail-related`.

misconception.myth: Secure Score fixes the tenant automatically and replaces admin judgment.
misconception.reality: Secure Score helps prioritize recommendations. Administrators still decide which actions fit risk, licensing, business impact, and rollout readiness.

lessons.examTakeaway: Map feature to symptom: MFA strengthens sign-in proof, Conditional Access applies policy, Defender for Office 365 handles email/collaboration threats, Secure Score prioritizes posture, and roles/PIM reduce privileged exposure.
lessons.recap: Identify MFA, Conditional Access, Defender for Office 365, Secure Score, admin roles, PIM, audit logs, app registrations, and enterprise applications.
lessons.simplerExplanation: Imagine airport operations: MFA checks passport plus boarding pass, Conditional Access chooses extra screening, Defender scans suspicious bags, Secure Score is the safety checklist, and admin roles control who enters the tower.
lessons.anotherExample: Adventure Works investigates a blocked finance sign-in by reading Conditional Access results, then assigns a reports-focused role instead of giving the analyst permanent Global Administrator access.
